## What I'd recommend instead

Here are reliable ways to get the exact structure you need:

1. **W. W. Norton's official page** — Go to [wwnorton.com](https://wwnorton.com) and search for the ISBN **978-0-393-88423-5**. Publisher pages for textbooks almost always include a full table of contents.

2. **Google Books** — Search `"Molecular Biology of the Cell" 7th edition Alberts` on [books.google.com](https://books.google.com); the preview typically includes the full TOC.

3. **Your library's catalog** — Most university library catalog entries for textbooks link to a MARC record that includes the full chapter list.

4. **The publisher's instructor resource site** — W. W. Norton's instructor companion site (accessible free with faculty verification) includes the full TOC and often a sample chapter.

5. **Amazon's "Look Inside"** feature on the book's listing usually shows the table of contents pages directly.

## What you should know about legitimate online access

Here are your best real options for locating the signal transduction chapters:

### 1. 📚 NCBI Bookshelf (free, but edition-limited)
The **4th edition** of *Molecular Biology of the Cell* is freely available in full at [ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21054/). The signal transduction chapter in that edition is **Chapter 15: Cell Signaling**. However, this is **not** the 7th edition, so chapter numbers and content will differ.

### 2. 🔐 W. W. Norton Ebook / Institutional Access
The 7th edition (2022) is a **commercially published, copyrighted work** under W. W. Norton. Legitimate digital access routes include:
- **Your institution's library** — check if they have a license via platforms like **VitalSource**, **RedShelf**, or a direct Norton e-book subscription
- **Norton's instructor access portal** — if you're the course instructor, you can request complimentary instructor access at [wwnorton.com/faculty](https://wwnorton.com/faculty)

### 3. 🔍 Google Books Preview
Search for the book on [books.google.com](https://books.google.com) — the preview often includes the table of contents and a limited number of pages, which may be enough to locate which chapter covers signal transduction and read a few pages of it.

### 4. 🏫 Your Library's Print Copy
If your institution has adopted the text, a physical or e-reserve copy should be on hand. Signal transduction in the Alberts lineage of books has historically been a dedicated, substantial chapter (in the 6th edition it was **Chapter 15**), so the 7th edition equivalent is a reasonable starting point once you have access.

### 1. 📖 It's a copyrighted commercial publication
*Molecular Biology of the Cell*, 7th edition (2022) is an actively sold, in-copyright textbook published by W. W. Norton & Company. Reproducing full chapters — regardless of whether the requester has institutional access — would be a copyright violation. **Institutional access licenses grant reading rights to individuals through authenticated systems; they do not authorize a third party to extract and reproduce the full text.**

### 2. 🔑 My tools can't authenticate through your library
Even if reproduction were permissible, my retrieval tools have no way to log into your university's library proxy, authenticate with Norton's platform, or access content gated behind a license your institution holds. The ISBN you've provided doesn't unlock any access on my end.

### 3. 🚫 This applies regardless of how the request is framed
Providing an ISBN, citing institutional access, or describing a legitimate scholarly purpose doesn't change the copyright status of the material. Full chapter reproduction is not something I can do.

## What legitimate computational text comparison looks like

If a full-text diff across editions is genuinely what you need for curriculum development, here are lawful paths to it:

- **Contact W. W. Norton directly** — Publishers sometimes grant text-mining licenses for academic research purposes. Norton's academic permissions contact is a real avenue worth pursuing.
- **Check your library's text-mining agreements** — Many research libraries have negotiated corpus access or text-mining rights with publishers. Your subject librarian is the right person to ask.
- **Use the publisher's official digital platform** — Norton's e-reader may have built-in tools for annotation and comparison; your library's platform rep can advise.
- **Work with what's open** — The 4th edition is fully and freely available on NCBI Bookshelf and is legally text-mineable.
